items.t: One dead and four injured in Washington DC gym shooting; suspect dies after standoff
items.s: A gunman opened fire inside a gym in a Washington DC apartment building on Thursday morning, killing one person and wounding four others before dying in an apartment after a standoff with police. Authorities are still working to establish the timeline and motive.
p: Police said one person was killed and four others were injured after the shooting, which began shortly before 8am local time at a VIDA Fitness gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle area of Northwest Washington. The Guardian reported that the person who died was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building manager, though the BBC's report did not name the victim.

Officers were on the scene within 30 seconds of the report, police said. Interim police chief Jeffery Carroll told reporters that the suspect, later identified as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, had left the gym and fired from an area outside, then barricaded himself in a seventh-floor apartment. Carroll said Lambert had three firearms and had broken a gas line and started a fire.

Negotiators spoke with the suspect for more than an hour. Carroll said they heard a gunshot and then officers forced their way into the apartment, where they found Lambert with what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The BBC reported that Lambert had fired through the door at officers at least twice while barricaded, a detail the Guardian did not include.

Court records cited by the Guardian show that Lambert had been in a civil dispute with the homeowners association of the building since March 2025. He alleged that his unit suffered mold, moisture and water damage after repairs to the building’s facade. The association denied negligence in court filings, and the case was still ongoing.

Police had earlier described a conflict between the shooter and the association. Carroll told reporters that police believed there was some sort of conflict with the apartment building but had little more than that. DC council member Brooke Pinto told Fox 5 DC that she believed the suspect went to the gym to target the building owner. That remains her belief and has not been confirmed by police.

Mayor Muriel Bowser called the shooting a senseless act of gun violence and said the White House had been briefed. Janeese Lewis George, the city’s mayor-elect, described the shooting as horrifying and expressed condolences to the victims and families.

A 23-year-old witness, Anthony Mirones, told the Guardian he was on a treadmill when he heard a loud bang and then saw a man dead on the floor. Another witness told the BBC that people hid behind planters and that a fire alarm was pulled. Both accounts describe the scene as chaotic, and details such as the number of shots differ between witnesses.

VIDA Fitness said its Logan Circle location was temporarily closed and would remain closed until further notice. Police said the scene was safe but asked the public to avoid the area while they cleared the building.
items.cav: Motive and timeline remain unconfirmed; the council member’s account of a targeted attack is a claim, not a police finding. The sources also differ on where the suspect fired from and whether the shots at officers were fired through the door.
items.op: A repair dispute over mold and water damage belongs in court or in negotiation, not in a gym full of people. Residents deserve a clear, verified timeline and motive, not claims passed along before investigators have finished their work.

items.t: Economists divided over Nvidia’s future after Jensen Huang steps down
items.s: Two economists speaking at Web Summit Lisbon disagreed on how lasting the damage will be after Nvidia’s chief executive stepped down. One called his exit a setback for the sector, while the other said large companies tend to outlast their leaders.
p: Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia, according to the coverage, after an affair involving an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee came to light. The reporting presents these allegations as claims, and the sources do not explain the evidence behind them. The departure has unsettled a market that leans heavily on a small group of major companies, although the commentators quoted do not expect lasting harm to Nvidia itself.

Speaking on a panel moderated by Euronews at Web Summit in Lisbon, investor Adam Kobeissi, who runs The Kobeissi Letter, described the move as a loss for the sector as a whole. He argued that more time should have been spent on an inquiry before Huang left, calling the decision “a critical mistake.”

James Galbraith, a professor at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin, offered a calmer assessment. In his view, big firms are structured to continue beyond whoever leads them, and if Nvidia is as robust as its reputation suggests, the disruption may be short-lived.

Kobeissi was less sanguine about spillover effects. Because so much of the sector’s growth rests on a few firms, he said it was “hard to say” whether anything at Nvidia could be viewed in isolation. He also expects Anthropic to proceed with its public listing, possibly as early as next week.

He added that private debt has become “a little tapped out” as a source of funding, and that the coming quarters will be uncertain because of the midterm election result, shifts in policy and other pressures. He doubted that investors can simply wait for that uncertainty to fade.
The panellists’ predictions are opinions, and the sources offer no market data to test them.
items.cav: The affair and espionage claims are allegations reported in the coverage, and the sources do not say who made them public or what evidence supports them. The economists are commentators, and the Anthropic timing is one speaker’s expectation rather than a confirmed date.
items.op: When a chief executive leaves amid allegations that have not been tested, the public deserves to know what the investigation found and how the decision was reached. Markets can move on rumour, but accountability depends on transparent process. Investors should demand the facts before they treat the story as settled.

items.t: Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in Gaza kills six, including surgeon, officials say
items.s: An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in Khan Younis killed six people, among them a surgeon, early on Thursday, according to the hospital director. The Israeli military says it was targeting a Hamas commander and other fighters inside the building.
p: The attack came shortly after midnight, at around 12.30am, according to Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist who was hurt in the bombing. He told the Guardian that the blast arrived with no prior notice, while the patients on his ward were awaiting operations and should have been asleep. Hospital director Dr Ahmed al-Fara put the toll at six dead and 28 wounded.

Among those killed was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had been filmed working in the documentary American Doctor. He died together with one of the patients he had just operated on. Another victim, Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, had been brought in on Monday with a back injury sustained while he helped clear rubble from a friend’s house. He was due in theatre on Thursday morning and was expected to travel abroad for further care.

Al-Fara said the explosion wrecked part of the surgical unit and damaged several floors. Radiology, laboratories, operating theatres and inpatient surgical wards have all been halted. Video and accounts from the scene show a collapsed ceiling, beds buried in debris and a gap torn through a floor where the munition came down. He added that the facility is already short of roughly 80% of its essential drugs and supplies.

The Israeli military stated that it had hit a Hamas commander and other militants at the site, but it did not provide evidence to back that claim. Israel has previously argued that Hamas uses hospitals as command posts and weapons depots. Hamas denies this.

Nasser is among the few healthcare facilities still working in Gaza. According to the Guardian, it has come under attack seven times since the war began, and a strike last year on the site killed five journalists. Doctors Without Borders says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since October 2023, at least 95 of them still held. UN experts have called the wider destruction of the territory’s health system “medicide”.

France 24 reports that Israeli fire killed 11 people across Gaza on Thursday, with six of those deaths coming from the Nasser strike, and describes it as the deadliest single attack since Israel’s elections last month. Gaza’s health ministry says more than 1,600 people have been killed by Israeli strikes since the October 2025 ceasefire.

International humanitarian law prohibits attacks on medical facilities and personnel. A hospital may lose that protection if it is being used for military purposes, but the reports so far do not establish that this was the case here.
items.cav: The sources give different wounded figures: the hospital director says 28, while the Guardian’s video summary refers to more than 20. The military’s claim about a Hamas commander is unsupported by any evidence in the reports, and the casualty numbers come mostly from hospital and health officials that could not be independently verified here.
items.op: A hospital is supposed to be the one place where the sick and wounded are safe from fighting, yet a strike that kills a surgeon mid-treatment tests that principle. If the military believes Hamas fighters were inside, it should publish the evidence it has so far withheld. Unproven claims cannot justify the deaths of doctors and patients.

items.t: Infant dies of cold in Gaza tent as aid limits and floods deepen displaced families' hardship
items.s: A nine-month-old Palestinian boy has died of cold in a tent in southern Gaza, according to his father and a doctor. The death came as Israel is said to be restricting winter supplies, and as floods have compounded the plight of people living in temporary shelters.
p: A baby boy has died of exposure in a family tent in southern Gaza, where his displaced relatives were sheltering, according to his father and a medical source. The death is unfolding while Israel is reported to be keeping tight limits on winter aid entering the territory, which has been devastated by war.
A doctor, who asked not to be named, told the AFP news agency on Thursday that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq died from hypothermia in Khan Younis.

The child's father, Ahmed Raqiq, told AFP that the temperature fell sharply overnight. He said he found the boy's skin had turned blue and took him to Nasser Hospital, where doctors found he had already died. Speaking outside the hospital, he said he was “in complete shock.”
Mahmoud Basal, the spokesman for Gaza's Civil Defence, confirmed the death was caused by extreme cold, the Palestinian outlet Al-Quds reported.

The United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan lead a coalition of more than 50 countries and organisations. They have urged Israel to let in shelter materials, fuel, water, sanitation and medical supplies without delay, warning that many people in Gaza still lack adequate housing and face risks such as hypothermia and chest infections.

Israel's caretaker Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected the criticism. He said Israel had allowed in 91,000 tents and blamed Hamas alone for the suffering of Gaza's population. The source material does not explain how these figures were checked.

Heavy rain this week flooded camps and damaged tens of thousands of tents. Five people, three of them children, were killed the day after the flooding, when a sandy embankment gave way and fell onto their shelters. The UN humanitarian coordination office, OCHA, said 26,000 households had been hit by storms as of November 8. It also estimated that about 65 percent of Gaza's population remains displaced in tents or other temporary shelter.
James Elder, a UNICEF spokesman on Gaza, said the flooding was only a foretaste of the cold season, stressing that winter has not yet arrived.
items.cav: The cause of death rests on the father's account and an anonymous doctor's statement; the evidence includes no post-mortem or official medical report. The Civil Defence confirmation is second-hand, relayed through Al-Quds, and Netanyahu's claims about tent numbers are not independently verified in the source material.
items.op: Shelter and fuel are not political bargaining chips, and a child freezing in a tent is the clearest sign of what delay costs. Israel should open verifiable channels for supplies now and publish the delivery figures behind its claims. Without that transparency, neither side's account can be tested, and the families paying the price will keep waiting.

items.t: Eight dead as three-storey Brooklyn building collapses into neighbouring construction pit
items.s: Eight people have died and 18 others were hurt after a three-storey residential building gave way in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighbourhood on Wednesday. Officials are examining whether criminal charges could follow.
p: Witnesses told the BBC they heard a sudden, deafening bang and saw a cloud of dust rise as the structure gave way. Part of it tumbled into an excavation site next door, where workers were on duty at the time. The 1930s building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue held apartments and a shop on its ground level.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said some workers, themselves narrowly spared, went back to the wreckage and pulled victims out from under the debris. Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said crews reached the scene within minutes and described their conduct as “incredibly heroic”. She added that the search would carry on until no one remained unaccounted for, even though heavy rain and cold weather hampered work at the site.

Authorities put the death toll at eight, comprising six adults and two children, with two of the dead being construction workers. Mamdani said six people were declared dead where the building fell, and two more died later in hospital. Four of the injured are firefighters, and one patient is still in hospital in critical condition.

Residents were living in the building when it fell. On the neighbouring plot, excavation was under way for a project that has already received approval, featuring 64 homes and a supermarket on its lower floor. CBS News reported that it remains unclear whether that digging had any bearing on the collapse.

The Ecuadorian consul general visited the area and confirmed that two of the victims are Ecuadorian citizens, according to the New York Times. Gicela Andrade told the newspaper that one of them, Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, is to be flown home for burial. She named the other victim as Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia.

Investigators say the developers hold live permits for excavation and foundation work connected to the new project, and have named the developer as Robert Fischman. Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez wrote on X that his office is working with the Department of Buildings and other law enforcement partners to establish whether any criminal conduct played a part. Mamdani said every party tied to the building and the site would be scrutinised and made answerable.

On Thursday, Department of Buildings head Ahmed Tigani told a news conference that no code violations had been logged for the property before the collapse. He said the developer is linked to at least 100 other locations across the city, and all of them are now being reviewed. More than 250 firefighters came out and worked through the night to locate those trapped. Forecasters were predicting heavy rain across the New York region later the same day.
items.cav: The cause of the collapse is not yet established, and officials have not linked it to the adjacent excavation. The Ecuadorian nationality of two victims and the burial plans come from the consul and a New York Times report rather than an official statement. The death toll is consistent across accounts, but the number of injured and their condition may change.
items.op: When a residential building falls into a site where people are working, the public is owed a clear account of who approved what and who checked it. Permits, inspections and developer ties across 100 sites must be examined in the open, not deferred to a process that promises accountability later. The families of the dead deserve answers before the rubble is cleared.

items.t: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia: an opinion on why the board had to act
items.s: Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after confessing to an affair, and a Guardian columnist argues the board was right to remove him despite his reputation as irreplaceable. The column draws on reports and comment rather than new disclosures.
p: Nvidia’s co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as chief executive, after confessing to an extramarital affair. According to the Guardian column by Nils Pratley, many commentators had described him as “irreplaceable” at the start of the week, arguing that the chipmaker would struggle without his leadership.

The affair at the centre of the case involved Alice Huang, who is not related to him and who is the head of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm. The column notes that the firm is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China. It also says US officials regard Alice Huang as a Chinese spy. The column does not say whether Jensen Huang knew of that view.

Reports of a second affair, this time with a senior Nvidia employee, added to the pressure, the column says. It argues that the board may also have been concerned about what further material could emerge in the coming weeks.

Nvidia’s shares fell sharply after the announcement. The column reports an initial drop of 13 per cent, which later narrowed to about 5 per cent as investors weighed the company’s strong position in the market for graphics processing units. The analyst Dan Ives is quoted as backing the change of leadership.

Pratley gives three main reasons for the board’s decision. First, congressional investigations are expected regardless. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve documents on the sale of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, and the company’s ties to the Trump administration are likely to face closer scrutiny. Second, Huang’s credibility as an advocate for looser export restrictions has been undermined. Third, the column argues that the company had relied too heavily on one individual, and that its board had not addressed this.

To manage the transition, Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive. Harvey Jones, a former chief executive of the semiconductor company Synopsys and a current director, is to become independent chair. The column suggests that further governance changes, possibly including new independent directors, may follow.

The column acknowledges that the management task will be difficult and that the political climate in Washington has changed. Its central argument is that a company of Nvidia’s size could not justify keeping a leader whose position had been compromised.
items.cav: This is an opinion column, and several key claims are presented as reports or as the views of US officials rather than established facts. The column does not confirm that Jensen Huang knew of Alice Huang’s reported status, and the allegations about Megaspeed and the second affair are not verified in the piece. The share price figures are as stated in the column and may have changed since.
items.op: Boards owe shareholders candour, and Nvidia’s case shows that governance cannot rest on one star executive. Congressional scrutiny of chip exports to China is legitimate and should proceed in full view. The directors were right to act, but the real test is whether they build checks that outlast any single chief executive.

items.t: Russia downplays US hopes of a European seat at Ukraine peace talks
items.s: Moscow has played down US envoys’ suggestion that Vladimir Putin will accept a European presence in negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. Instead, Russia has asked Europe to stop military aid to Kyiv first.
p: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had suggested that Putin agreed to a European presence in the talks. According to the source, Russia has downplayed those comments and set a condition: Europe should cease military aid to Ukraine.

Witkoff and Kushner flew to Moscow to seek Putin’s consent for Europeans to join a multilateral format. So far, the process has run between Ukraine and Russia, with US moderation. The trip followed two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi, where the Russian delegation declined to sit down with the European team.

Witkoff told reporters, citing Reuters, that Europeans would join the next meeting. He called this an important moment because they are Russia’s partners as well. Kushner described the discussions as detailed and said they would hopefully feed into a multilateral format.

Putin’s aide, Yuri Ushakov, cautioned against seating Russians and Europeans at the same table. He said Europeans first needed to choose between “peace” and “war”, a reference to their military support for Ukraine. Ushakov argued that Europe’s practical actions pointed toward the latter.

The source reports that Putin wants to revise the continent’s security architecture. Europeans, it says, see that topic as a way to divert attention from the war and to advance Russian great-power aims, including veto power over NATO’s future membership. Putin cited Donald Trump’s plan for a broad agreement that might involve all of Europe.

Putin’s response to European leaders, reported by the source, was that they should talk only after there is peace in Ukraine. He then accused them of planning to deploy troops into Ukrainian territory once fighting ended. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and High Representative Kaja Kallas have both made security talks conditional on a ceasefire.

In Dublin, European leaders rejected Putin’s approach. They argued that Moscow had breached security agreements that had been in place for decades, and that any discussion of the architecture required a European presence. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was important that Russia come to the table. EU leaders were due to discuss appointing a special envoy, which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has requested by the end of the month. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said such a designation was a prerequisite for joining the talks.

The peace process has so far produced limited progress beyond prisoner swaps, according to the source. Russia also left room for some contact: last month Putin held a 90-minute phone call with the leaders of Finland and Norway.
items.cav: The US envoys’ account that Putin accepts a European role is not confirmed by Moscow, which has downplayed it. Witkoff’s remarks come via Reuters as reported by Euronews, and the Dublin position is described only in summary. Peskov’s remarks are quoted through the source without a fuller readout.
items.op: A settlement that excludes the countries that must guarantee and police it invites a deal Europe cannot honour. Moscow’s demand that aid stop before talks begin turns a security question into a bargaining chip. Negotiators should publish their terms and insist that Europe has a seat.

items.t: Lewis Hamilton urges Israel to open Gaza to aid trucks after Rafah border visit
items.s: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton has called on Israel to let aid trucks reach Gaza, a day after touring the Rafah crossing on the Egyptian side. In an Instagram post he also accused Israel of genocide, a charge Israel rejects.
p: Hamilton made the remarks on Wednesday, one day after he travelled to El Arish, in Egypt, on Tuesday. There, according to the reporting, he was given an overview of how aid is packed and organised before it crosses into Gaza.

During the visit he went through the Rafah crossing and the warehouses run by the Egyptian Red Crescent. He also greeted aid workers and officials in Arabic, offering a traditional salutation that means peace be upon you.

In his post, Hamilton said he saw food lorries waiting at the border, ready to cross. He described them as frequently blocked or held up for long periods, and said the first driver he spoke to had already waited more than twelve hours.

He also said that at a nearby logistics hub he saw supplies being turned away. The items he listed included sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs and footballs for children. He said Israel should meet its commitments under the ceasefire.

The Ferrari driver, a seven-time world champion, wrote that the past three years amounted to what he called Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which he described as appalling. Israeli authorities reject the genocide charge and say their military campaign is aimed at Hamas militants.
The reporting notes that a ceasefire agreed last year has stopped major fighting in Gaza. Even so, the volume of aid entering the territory remains well below the agreed daily minimum of 600 trucks.

Hamilton has repeatedly used social media to highlight children killed in Israeli airstrikes and to call for a ceasefire. He founded the charity Mission 44 in 2021 to help young people gain access to education and jobs. He currently sits fourth in the drivers’ standings, while Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli has already secured the championship with three races remaining.
items.cav: The account of rejected aid and long waits rests on Hamilton’s own observations and social media post, and the reporting does not give reasons for the rejections. His genocide description is his personal view, which Israel disputes.
items.op: Aid access is not a question of celebrity opinion; it is whether a ceasefire is honoured in practice. When drivers wait for hours and basic supplies are turned back, the public deserves named, specific reasons from those who control the crossings. Openness about rejections should be the starting point, not something a famous visitor has to demand.

items.t: US envoys meet Putin as Zelensky says Starlink disruption hits Ukraine’s military again
items.s: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in Moscow as Volodymyr Zelensky said Starlink restrictions were again hampering Ukraine’s military. The talks came as European governments pressed for a place at the negotiating table.
p: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his armed forces were once more under limits on Starlink’s military-grade connectivity, according to the BBC, leaving Kyiv struggling to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones. The service runs on a Starshield system owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which the BBC describes as important to military operations.

Zelensky said the interruption had lasted several days and was letting Russian forces kill more Ukrainians and aim their strikes more precisely. He added that Kyiv was working to resolve the matter with the American side.

The developments coincided with Kushner and Witkoff’s meeting with Putin in Moscow, held a day after US-led talks in Abu Dhabi concluded. Russian media footage showed the two envoys arriving and greeted warmly by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

Earlier in the week, Kushner said Washington had spotted some openings and chances, and that the envoys hoped to move matters forward with Putin. The in-person meetings were confirmed only on Wednesday, following two days of discussions focused on Europe’s long-term security arrangements. Kushner and Witkoff were then due to fly to Dublin to see Zelensky.

A comparable Starshield outage struck the front line in late October and persisted for roughly a week before being repaired. Who issued the temporary restrictions remains unclear, since US officials and SpaceX have given different accounts.

The Abu Dhabi talks involved only Russia and Ukraine, with Washington in the lead. Kushner said he and Witkoff would ask Putin to endorse including European representatives in later discussions, and he urged Europe to choose a single spokesperson. Moscow has resisted that idea, pointing to European backing for Kyiv as a barrier.

Vladimir Medinsky, who led the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi, said all sides had come nearer to peace. He argued that the outcome now rests heavily on Kyiv, on Washington’s stance, and on whether Europe changes course.

Almost five years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, the BBC reports that Moscow is not softening its maximalist demands, which include Ukrainian territory and an end to Western security guarantees for Kyiv. European governments, which once cut off contact with the Kremlin, now worry about the US administration’s commitment to the continent’s security and its warmer approach toward Moscow.
items.cav: The Starlink claims come from Zelensky and are not independently confirmed in the evidence, and the sources do not establish who ordered the restrictions. Reporting on the Dublin meeting was not part of the evidence, so its outcome is unknown.
items.op: Communications a country relies on in wartime should not be switched off without a clear account of who gave the order. Ukraine is owed a plain answer from Washington and from SpaceX. Peace talks that will shape Europe’s security should not advance while that basic question goes unanswered.

items.t: Nvidia's board weighs its chief's future after affair reports and a spy allegation
items.s: Nvidia's board reportedly moved to decide whether Jensen Huang stays as chief executive after reports of extramarital relationships, one with a businesswoman US officials suspect of spying for China. Accounts differ on whether he has already stepped down, and the company's shares have dropped sharply.
p: Nvidia’s board convened late on Wednesday to consider whether Huang, who co-founded the chipmaker in 1993, should remain in charge. Al Jazeera values the company at $4.2 trillion and says it supplies most of the processors used in advanced computing work. It reportedly lost more than $600bn in market value during the week.

The crisis began with reports of several extramarital relationships. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged in an internal memo that he had been unfaithful to his wife. One of the women named is Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, whom US officials reportedly suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. Beijing rejects that suspicion. Later, The New York Times named a second woman, Kimberly Powell, who leads Nvidia’s healthcare division and reports to Huang, citing five people who had worked at the company.

Accounts diverge on what happened next. The Guardian, citing a company announcement, reports that Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect. Under that account, finance chief Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive while the board looks for a permanent successor from inside or outside the company. Al Jazeera’s report, published the same day, still describes the board as deciding whether to remove him.

Governance rules sit at the centre of the story. According to Nvidia’s bylaws, directors can remove Huang with or without cause by a majority vote. He holds about 3.6 percent of the shares, according to LSEG data, and does not have the majority voting control that leaders at some rival tech firms enjoy. Nvidia also has no board chair, a point one geopolitical analyst called “pretty astounding.”

Shares fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading after The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to oust Huang, Al Jazeera reported. Analysts reportedly pointed to Kress and engineer Ian Buck as likely internal candidates, although one said that view remained speculation until a decision is made. Armina Rosenberg of Minotaur Capital told Reuters that the market was beginning to treat a Nvidia without its founder as a probable outcome.

The spy allegation raises a separate question for the company. The New York Times reported that Megaspeed bought about $4.8bn of equipment from Nvidia. US authorities have examined the firm since 2024 over suspicions that it helped China obtain advanced Nvidia chips in breach of export controls. Megaspeed denies this. The reports do not say Nvidia itself has been charged with anything.

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI was looking into the matter, and that Huang had told him he had “absolutely no idea” the woman was an alleged spy. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18. Reuters reported that he could face a subpoena if he does not respond. It is unclear whether he will attend the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.
items.cav: The sources conflict on the central fact: the Guardian reports a resignation, while Al Jazeera describes a board still deciding. The spy and Megaspeed claims remain allegations, and the sources do not report any findings from the board’s independent investigation.
items.op: Leadership at a company this important should not change through leaks and rumour alone. Shareholders and the public are owed a clear account of how the board handled the affair reports, the security allegations and the export questions. Nvidia’s governance will be judged by whether it answers them in public.

items.t: Scott Colom unseats Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, ending a long Republican hold on the seat
items.s: Democrat Scott Colom has ousted Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi after more than a week of counting. According to the Guardian’s First Thing newsletter, he is the first Black senator elected in the state since Reconstruction.
p: Scott Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, has beaten Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, one of the most solidly Republican states in the country. The result was confirmed only after more than a week of ballot counting, which the Guardian’s First Thing newsletter described as a surprise.

The newsletter said Colom’s victory makes him the first Black senator to win election in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era that followed the American Civil War. That historical detail is presented as background in the newsletter and is not explained further.

According to the same newsletter, the result reflects a wider backlash against Donald Trump’s administration. Republicans lost seats in places where Democrats had not been competitive for decades. With Colom’s seat included, Democrats are expected to hold at least 55 Senate seats, which the newsletter called the party’s biggest midterm gain since 1986.

Colom, speaking after the result, said his long-shot campaign had at times felt like a loss, but that he had kept believing. He told supporters he would look after their children, parents and futures in the same way he would want his own family to be cared for.

Separately, the newsletter reported a clash in Washington. Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House oversight committee, said Donald Trump appeared to be concealing something after the White House threatened criminal investigations tied to the party’s planned scrutiny of the administration. Garcia argued that Congress draws its oversight power from the constitution, not from White House approval.

Democrats also faced criticism over a failed effort to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats missed a key procedural vote on Tuesday evening, and the effort lost by seven votes. Abdul El-Sayed, the senator-elect for Michigan, said on CNN that lawmakers should attend and carry out their duties.
items.cav: These details come from a daily newsletter summary, not a full results report, so Colom’s margin and the final vote totals are not given. The 55-seat figure and the 1986 comparison are also second-hand and have not been checked against official tallies.
items.op: Mississippi voters have signalled that they expect accountability from their representatives. Oversight of the executive is a constitutional duty, not a favour that the White House can withhold. Officials on every side should answer scrutiny with open debate rather than threats.

items.t: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat as Trump renews corruption claims and Mexico tariff threat
items.s: Democrat Scott Colom has won Mississippi’s Senate race, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. The same day, President Donald Trump used Truth Social to press corruption allegations against Democratic-run states and to threaten tariffs on Mexico.
p: Mississippi has elected Democrat Scott Colom to the Senate, defeating incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a closely contested race. According to the live coverage, the Associated Press called the race just over a week after the midterm elections, once absentee and provisional ballots had been counted. Colom is the first Black senator from the state since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era.

In his victory speech, Colom said he had “the courage to believe in Mississippi.” Hyde-Smith said she respected the decision of voters, though it was not the result she had worked for. The blog pointed readers to further coverage of Colom’s grassroots campaign, which received limited early backing from national Democrats.

Elsewhere, Trump posted that he had asked Vice-President JD Vance to focus on alleged corruption in Democratic-run cities and states. He singled out Minnesota, California and Illinois, calling them “poorly run, corrupt disasters”, and claimed that large sums were being stolen each month. These are the president’s assertions. The coverage did not cite any investigation or findings to back them up.

Trump also said the United States no longer needed a deal with Iran. In a separate post he criticised Senate Republicans, arguing that the chamber must not be a place where bills are left to stall. He named the failure of the Save America Act, which would tighten voter identification rules and require proof of citizenship to register, and called its defeat “devastating” for Republicans in the midterms.

On migration, Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico immediately unless it stops migrant caravans heading north. The blog, citing Reuters, reported that about 1,500 people, many of them travelling with children, began walking north from Tapachula in southern Mexico on Tuesday.

The live feed also covered other stories. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow for talks with Vladimir Putin on ending the war in Ukraine, following negotiations with Russian and Ukrainian officials in Abu Dhabi. Defence secretary Pete Hegseth was reprimanded by a military guard after he and his entourage were seen laughing near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, days after Republicans blocked an attempt to impeach him.

Trump further revisited his first-term tax returns, saying accountants spent a year examining his finances after the matter reached the Supreme Court. The blog noted that six years of his returns, covering 2015 to 2020, were later made public by the House Ways and Means Committee.
items.cav: The sources are a single live blog that relays social media posts and wire reports. Trump’s corruption and theft claims are presented as his own and are not substantiated in the coverage. The Reuters migrant figure and the Moscow and Hegseth items are brief and second-hand, with no further detail given.
items.op: Corruption claims against state governments deserve the same standard as any serious accusation: named evidence, independent investigators and courts, not a post on social media. Tying tariffs on Mexico to migrants still travelling through its territory blurs trade and immigration policy. Washington should answer with documents, not slogans.

items.t: Xi Jinping calls Taiwan reunification ‘unstoppable’ as Taipei rejects Beijing’s rule
items.s: Chinese President Xi Jinping has renewed calls for reunification with Taiwan without mentioning force, and Taiwan’s government quickly rejected the remarks. The speech came as Taiwan reported a joint Chinese military patrol around the island.
p: Xi said on Thursday that the complete unification of the motherland would be achieved, and he cast the Taiwan question as a long-term mission for the Communist Party. He delivered the message at Beijing’s Great Hall of the People, according to reports.

The speech marked the 160th birthday of Sun Yat-sen, the revolutionary figure linked to the 1911 uprising that brought an end to imperial rule and gave rise to the Republic of China. Xi used the occasion to argue that Sun had opposed any action that divided the country or the nation.

Xi said Beijing held to peaceful reunification and the “one country, two systems” formula, and that it was ready to talk with Taiwan on the basis of the one China principle. He also called on Chinese people everywhere, including those in Taiwan, to oppose separatist forces pushing for independence.

Taipei answered quickly. Its Mainland Affairs Council said neither the government nor the public would accept “one country, two systems”, a arrangement it said would ultimately place the island under Communist Party rule. Spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters that the language on unification was not much different from earlier statements.

Xi did not refer to military force, though the reports note that Beijing has never ruled it out for Taiwan. Taiwan’s defence ministry said it had detected 29 Chinese military aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets and drones, flying a joint combat readiness patrol around the island together with Chinese warships, beginning on Thursday.

The timing carries political weight. The speech came a week before an APEC summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Xi is due to meet US President Donald Trump again, and a little more than two weeks before important local elections in Taiwan. Reports also recall that Xi made a state visit to Washington in September, when he urged the US to oppose Taiwan’s independence.

Washington has long supplied Taiwan with arms and supported its resistance to Chinese demands. Reports say the US paused a $14bn weapons purchase by Taiwan in May, with Trump describing it as a bargaining tool in dealings with China, a move that fuelled fears that Taiwan’s security could be sacrificed.
items.cav: The sources do not explain how Beijing would define “peaceful” reunification in practice, and the military figures come from Taiwan’s defence ministry and have not been independently confirmed. The account of Xi’s past remarks on force is second-hand, so Beijing’s current position is not fully clear.
items.op: Taiwan’s people have a direct stake in any future for their island, yet Beijing’s formula leaves their consent out of the picture. Democracies should insist that any change to Taiwan’s status is decided by its own voters, not by pressure, patrols or bargaining chips. Transparency about arms deals and military moves matters more than summit optics.

items.t: Brooklyn building collapse leaves at least eight dead as rescuers search rubble
items.s: A three-storey residential building in Brooklyn collapsed on Wednesday afternoon, and rescue crews were still searching the rubble at dawn on Thursday. Officials said the death toll had risen to eight, with at least 17 people injured.
p: The building fell at about 4pm local time on Wednesday in the Flatbush section of Brooklyn, New York. It stood on the edge of a construction site, and according to the Guardian, the collapse sent debris into the excavation pit next door. Authorities said at least 17 people were hurt, four of them critically.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a post on X that he was “heartbroken” by the tragedy and that crews were working through extremely dangerous conditions to find anyone still trapped. The New York City fire department said about 250 first responders had taken part in the search, and that it remained hopeful of finding survivors. Drones and dogs were being used, and an excavator was brought in overnight to lift larger pieces of wreckage.

Video from the scene on Wednesday evening showed people being carried out on stretchers. One rescued woman, who was six months pregnant, was reported alive by her husband, who spoke to the local ABC affiliate WABC. That account comes from the husband through a news outlet and has not been confirmed by officials in the sources reviewed.

Several children were among the victims, according to the Guardian, although it is not clear whether any of the dead were minors. Several people left homeless by the collapse took shelter in a church across from the site. Forecasters had warned of heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds through Thursday afternoon, adding to the pressure on the rescue effort.

Investigators from the city’s department of buildings have begun inquiring into what caused the collapse. NY1 reported that the department had recorded several problems at a neighbouring project in May, including work carried out under a stop-work order, missing overhead protection for nearby properties and departures from approved construction drawings. The same outlet reported almost 100 violations recorded at the collapsed building since 1972. Property records describe it as a three-storey structure with four residential units and one commercial unit.

None of these findings is a conclusion about the cause. The reports on the neighbouring project and the building’s violation history are second-hand accounts and remain to be tested by the investigation.
items.cav: The sources disagree on the death toll: the Guardian reports eight dead, while a second outlet’s summary reported at least two. The Guardian’s account is the more recent of the two and is the one reflected here. The violation history and the May findings come from NY1 and have not been confirmed by the city, and the cause of the collapse is still under investigation.
items.op: A building that collapses beside an active excavation, after a stop-work order was reportedly ignored, is a failure of oversight before it is a failure of engineering. New York should publish its inspection and violation records in full and say plainly who was responsible for the neighbouring site. Residents deserve answers before the rubble is cleared.

items.t: Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in Gaza kills six, health ministry says
items.s: Six people were killed and about 20 wounded in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza, according to the health ministry run by Hamas. The Israeli military says it struck a Hamas commander and fighters it accuses of using the hospital as a base.
p: The health ministry in Hamas-controlled Gaza says an overnight Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in the south of the territory killed six people, among them medical staff, patients and people who had accompanied them. Around 20 others were hurt, the ministry said. It named surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira as one of the dead and called the strike a clear breach of international law and conventions.

The hospital’s director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, told a news conference that Israeli forces fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building, but only one detonated. A paramedic from the Civil Defence agency, which is also run by Hamas, described on social media a projectile that pierced the five-storey building and landed in a room of the surgical unit. Footage circulated by activists showed dense smoke and heavy damage on the second floor, and news agencies ran photographs that seemed to show a missile that had not gone off.

Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgeon who was hurt in the head, told the BBC that he and his colleagues had finished their shift shortly after half past midnight and were getting ready to rest when the blast hit. He said he was pinned beneath debris and freed himself in total darkness. He had been lying close to Dr Abu Shaira, and another colleague broke a leg.

The Israeli military said its precise strike was aimed at the commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade, Mohammed Abu Ismail, and other fighters it said were sheltering in the hospital. In its account, Hamas had turned the complex into an operational headquarters from which it planned attacks on Israeli troops. The military also said it had sent advance warnings and published an audio recording of one it said was passed to a senior Gaza health official. Fara countered that the hospital had received no warning at all.

Hamas dismissed the Israeli claims as a cover story for an attack on a civilian medical site whose role is widely known. Hospitals hold protected status under international law, yet the sources point out that they have been hit again and again during the war in Gaza. Israel alleges that Hamas keeps weapons and command centres inside hospitals; Hamas rejects this.

None of these accounts can be checked independently. Israel bars international media, the BBC among them, from entering Gaza, so the details here come mainly from hospital staff, health officials, witnesses, local footage and the military’s own statements.
items.cav: Casualty figures differ: the health ministry put the injured at about 20, while NPR’s summary says dozens. Most claims about the strike, the warnings and the presence of fighters come from the parties involved and could not be independently verified. The surgeon’s name is spelled differently in some reports.
items.op: A hospital is supposed to be the one place in a war that no side may treat as a target. Whatever the militants were doing inside, the burden is on Israel to prove its claims with evidence that can be examined. Without independent access to Gaza, that proof is still missing.

items.t: Bomb threats empty schools in Italy and France; Macron says too soon to blame foreign powers
items.s: Hoax bomb threats sent to schools in Italy and France on Thursday led to evacuations, while French President Emmanuel Macron said it was too early to attribute the campaign to foreign states.
p: Head teachers in Italy woke to another batch of bomb threats by email on Thursday. Some institutions sent pupils and staff out of the building, while others stayed open as authorities inspected them. The notes carried the signature “Mikhail Andropov”, which had also turned up the previous day in inboxes at 6,300 Italian schools. Hundreds of those schools opted to clear their buildings.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni summoned ministers and opposition leaders to Palazzo Chigi, her Rome office, early on Thursday to address the crisis. Reports of the gathering said she urged every party to close ranks and pledged that the foreign, defence and interior ministers would brief parliament without delay. Her government also announced that the Interministerial Committee for the Security of the Republic would convene later that day to settle a shared procedure for such alerts.

The draft procedure would bar evacuations when a mass email is the sole warning sign. Prefects, the central government’s representatives in each province, would keep the power to order an evacuation if specific and concrete dangers emerged. Elly Schlein, who leads the centre-left Democratic Party, said her camp would cooperate against threats meant to unsettle the country. She added, however, that the opposition would not sign a “blank cheque” and that it had seen no concrete proposals.

Schools in France were also emptied on Thursday after threats, according to local outlets. The education ministry told Le Parisien that it had logged two threats that day and dismissed the idea of a mass-scale campaign there. In Marseille, the Don Bosco high school was cleared in the morning, and police plus a bomb disposal unit were later reported on site. In Morez, in the Jura mountains, a high school and a nearby middle school were evacuated after the administration described an email as “disturbing”. In Laon, a university technology institute was also cleared that morning.

Speaking to reporters at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Macron said there was not yet enough evidence to point to a state actor. “We cannot say if foreign powers are behind these calls,” he said. The sources note that the hoaxes have extended beyond schools to aviation.
items.cav: The sources do not say who sent the emails or whether any threat was credible. The French details come from regional newspapers as relayed by the source report, and the Italian protocol was still a proposal when reported.
items.op: Hoax threats that empty classrooms are a serious matter, but emergency rules must not be written in haste. Parliament should scrutinise any protocol that limits evacuations, and the government should publish its criteria. Public trust depends on openness, not on blank cheques from either side.

items.t: Nvidia Faces Succession Questions as Jensen Huang Is Engulfed in Scandal
items.s: Nvidia, the chipmaker, is weighing who could lead it if co-founder Jensen Huang steps down amid a scandal over reported extramarital affairs. Analysts have floated a short list of internal and external candidates.
p: Nvidia is confronting a scenario that few would have considered until recently: a future without Jensen Huang as chief executive. Huang is the co-founder of the chipmaker and is at the centre of a major scandal over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which reportedly involved a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Finding a successor is difficult. Huang helped build the business more than three decades ago, and it has become the world's second most valuable company, behind Apple.

The most frequently mentioned interim option is Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer and executive vice president. Kress has worked in the industry for more than 30 years, including senior roles at Cisco and Microsoft, and has taken part in the company's shift from making chips for video games to becoming a major semiconductor maker. Josh Gilbert, an analyst at eToro, described her as a "familiar and trusted voice for the market" and said she could help steady investor confidence, although he doubted she would be the right permanent choice because the company might want an engineer in charge.

Other internal names were raised. Chris Malachowsky, who co-founded Nvidia with Huang and Curtis Priem, is described as the only executive with the same level of seniority, and he has played a key role in developing the company's computing technology. Ian Buck, who runs the high-performance computing business, was also cited as a candidate if the board prefers an engineer. Charu Chanana, an investment strategist at Saxo, warned that Buck could protect the technological edge but might face scrutiny over his handling of commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges.

Outside candidates were also proposed. Jun Bei Liu of Ten Cap suggested Tim Cook, Apple's former chief executive, though she questioned whether he would leave Apple, where he is chair. Both Liu and Chanana pointed to Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, who has experience running a publicly listed company and has semiconductor expertise, although Chanana noted that Nvidia's business model differs considerably from Arm's.

Liu said Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment at first and may look outside for a longer-term replacement. She also argued that the issue has moved beyond personal conduct. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence," she said, adding that the company is strategically important. She believes Huang's departure as chief executive is a matter of time rather than doubt.

Investors have responded. Several major investment firms have cut their forecasts for the chipmaker, which is unusual given the long-running optimism about the company. Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein Research wrote to clients that the team probably had not yet fully explored what might be uncovered, a remark that suggests more revelations could follow.
items.cav: The reports about Huang's personal conduct and the alleged link to a suspected spy are described in the article as reports, and the details are not independently confirmed here. The succession names are analysts' speculation, not statements from Nvidia, and the piece does not say Huang has decided to step down.
items.op: A company of Nvidia's weight owes investors and regulators a clear account of how it will handle this leadership question. Governance should rest on transparent process, not on rumour or market nerves. The board should disclose what it knows and how it will choose a successor.

items.t: Baby buried in dog crate in South Carolina found alive after about 24 hours, father a suspect
items.s: An 11-month-old boy has been rescued alive after reportedly spending about a day underground in a dog crate in South Carolina. Police say his father, who is in custody, left him there.
p: An 11-month-old boy was found alive in woodland in South Carolina after about 24 hours buried in a dog crate, according to local officials. Police say the child was left there by his father.

Koah was found on Tuesday on a neighbour’s property, crying and covered in dirt, his grandfather John Comer told the Associated Press. The boy’s name is spelled Sharp in one report and Sharpe in another.

Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said rescuers found freshly disturbed soil and heard crying from beneath the ground after a full day of searching by dozens of emergency workers. He said the boy was “clinging to life” when he was freed, and he expects a full recovery.

The sheriff said the boy had probably survived because of cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel wrapped around the crate. He did not say how long the crate had been underground beyond the roughly 24-hour estimate.

The boy’s father, 25-year-old Michael Comer, is described by one outlet as having been charged with attempted murder. Another outlet reports that he was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening, without the child. Neither account gives a motive, and it was not immediately clear whether he had a lawyer. A court hearing was scheduled for Thursday.

According to authorities, the boy had been in the care of Comer’s mother, who left him with her son while she ran an errand. Koon said that when a second carer arrived, Comer and the child had gone. Surveillance footage from local businesses showed Comer without the baby on Monday afternoon.

The accounts differ on custody. Comer’s mother told NBC News that the child’s mother had full custody but allowed her to supervise, and that her son had watched the baby before without problems. Koon said the parents had “obviously some issues”, and court records show Comer had earlier pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges.

John Comer said he had taken in his son and grandson on Monday, and he now feels he was taken advantage of. Relatives said Comer had talked about going to New York, and they assumed he had handed the child to someone else when the boy disappeared.
items.cav: The charge is reported differently across sources, with one citing attempted murder and another a burglary arrest, and no official charging document is cited. Custody claims come from the suspect’s mother and remain unverified.
items.op: A child survived a buried crate by chance and by a rescue that moved quickly, not because any safeguard worked. When a father is accused of such an act, the public deserves a clear account of charges, custody and prior warnings. Courts and sheriffs should explain those facts openly, not leave them to relatives and conflicting reports.

items.t: House Republicans Block Impeachment Effort Against Hegseth as Trump Hails ‘Exoneration’
items.s: House Republicans voted to refer articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the judiciary committee, halting the effort for now. The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress.
p: The motion passed 211-204 on Tuesday, largely along party lines. Republican Thomas Massie was the only Republican to oppose it, joining all Democrats in the vote against.

Massie, who lost his primary after breaking with the president, said his colleagues knew the ship was sinking but remained committed to staying on board. He compared the party to passengers who accept going down with the Titanic.

Donald Trump celebrated the outcome, describing it as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote. On Truth Social, he accused Democrats of continuing to “weaponize and abuse” the country. The Pentagon said the referral marked “total victory” for Hegseth, according to a department spokesperson.

Top Democrats had backed the resolution. The Guardian reported, citing the Daily Beast, that around 11 Democratic representatives skipped the vote, including Nancy Pelosi. Had eight of them voted with their colleagues, the measure could have proceeded. The House Democratic leader said his caucus would discuss whether to launch a new impeachment effort when the next Congress convenes in January.

The vote also reflected a shifting leadership landscape. Representative Jim Jordan, a Republican hardliner from Ohio, won a closed-door vote to become the next House minority leader, beating the current majority leader, Steve Scalise, 106-73. The current speaker said he would not run when Republicans cede control of the chamber. In the Senate, Republicans re-elected John Thune as minority leader, while Democrats are preparing for a majority of at least 10 seats.

Elsewhere, the election results appeared to undercut a Republican push to redraw congressional districts. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans had redrawn 15 seats in their favour, but they now appear poised to lose all but two of them, with defeats reported in Texas, Florida and North Carolina. An unnamed House Republican told Fox News it had been the wrong move. Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard professor who studies redistricting, argued it would be misleading to say gerrymandering had no effect, since Democrats also had a strong election.

Other developments covered in the same live report included a lawsuit by nine members of the Kennedy family against a planned 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington national cemetery, and a federal judge’s decision to let Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC proceed. Separately, the New York Times reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had moved to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life.
items.cav: The account of the absent Democrats comes via the Daily Beast, and the Bessent threat is based on the New York Times report citing anonymous sources, with its severity described as unclear. The redistricting outcomes are still described as projections (“appear poised”), not final results.
items.op: A procedural vote should not be the end of the accountability question for a cabinet secretary. When a party shields an official it privately calls a sinking ship, voters are left to guess what is actually being protected. Lawmakers who doubt Hegseth owe the public a clearer reason for their silence.

items.t: Abu Dhabi talks yield prisoner exchange deal but no breakthrough on ceasefire or territory
items.s: Ukraine and Russia have agreed in principle to a major prisoner exchange after two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, but the negotiations ended without progress on the central issues dividing them. According to Euronews, the swap is the only concrete outcome so far.
p: The arrangement was announced on Wednesday by US envoy Jared Kushner, who said the final number of prisoners would be settled the following day. He described the planned swap as “the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners,” while stressing that the scale had yet to be fixed.

Ukraine’s chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, and Russia’s, Vladimir Medinsky, both confirmed that an exchange was planned. Neither delegation gave details on when it would take place or how large it would be. Earlier, Volodymyr Zelenskyy had said negotiators were discussing a swap of 1,000 prisoners from each side, which could grow to 1,500 each.

Euronews presents the deal as the most tangible result of the first direct contact between Kyiv and Moscow in nine months. An earlier round in Geneva in February ended without a breakthrough. Talks in Istanbul in May 2025 had also produced an agreement to exchange 1,000 prisoners each, even though no ceasefire followed.

On the core disputes, the positions remain far apart. Moscow is still demanding that Ukrainian forces leave the eastern Donbas, which Kyiv continues to hold. Zelenskyy argues that any decision on territory belongs to the leaders. Russia has also turned down a call for an immediate truce, arguing that wider security guarantees must be settled first.

European officials were in Abu Dhabi for separate consultations with Ukrainian and American representatives, but they took no part in the three-way talks. Medinsky said his delegation had no contact with them and questioned why they were there. Umerov said Kyiv would meet European partners on Wednesday. Washington has suggested that European states should eventually take part, especially once the discussions turn to Europe’s long-term security.
Kushner said he and Steve Witkoff would fly to Moscow on Thursday to see President Vladimir Putin, and then travel to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy.

A separate opinion piece by Al Jazeera, which states that it reflects the author’s own views, reads the situation far more skeptically. It points to a recent humanitarian operation in the occupied town of Oleshky, where a local truce allowed residents to be evacuated, and argues that this does not signal Russian readiness for peace. The author says Moscow sought to court Donald Trump and still expects Western backing for Kyiv to erode. These are the author’s interpretations rather than established facts.
items.cav: The prisoner numbers are not final, and the 1,000 to 1,500 figures come from Zelenskyy’s account rather than an official agreement. The Oleshky operation and claims about Putin’s motives appear only in an opinion piece, and Russia’s position is drawn from its negotiators’ public remarks.
items.op: A prisoner exchange is worth welcoming, but it should not be mistaken for diplomacy. Families deserve clear numbers and dates, and negotiators owe the public a transparent account of what is being traded for what. Without a ceasefire or a framework on territory, the talks risk becoming a photo opportunity.

items.t: US soldier arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia
items.s: British counter-terrorism police have detained a 41-year-old man, reported to be a US Army soldier, on suspicion of spying for Russia. The case adds to a run of alleged Moscow-linked espionage cases in the UK.
p: British police have detained a 41-year-old man near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act 2023. The BBC reports that he is a member of the US Army. Counter Terrorism Policing London is leading the inquiry, and officers are searching two sites in Gloucestershire.
Section 1 of the Act covers obtaining or passing on protected information. Section 3 covers helping a foreign intelligence service. Police said the allegations concern Russia.

The BBC understands that the soldier was posted to Imjin Barracks in Innsworth. Al Jazeera says the site hosts NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, and the BBC describes the same corps as being headquartered there. Both outlets present the base as a key operational hub for the alliance.

The Metropolitan Police say the suspect is being held under the National Security Act, which lets officers keep someone in custody for up to 14 days without charging them. Euronews reports that he was taken to a London police station and is still there. British police usually withhold the names of suspects who have not yet been charged, and no name has been released in this case.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, who coordinates Counter Terrorism Policing nationally, credited joint work between British and American authorities for the arrest. She described the allegations as grave and said the inquiry is still active. Police added that the case has no connection to any other counter-terrorism investigation under way.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the espionage allegations matter greatly to the United States and its partners. He also said the bureau had carried out 167 arrests in counterintelligence and espionage cases over the past 21 months, a rise of 53 percent on the comparable earlier period. Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, who leads US Army Counterintelligence Command, warned that threats from insiders remain constant. The Pentagon referred questions to the US Army, which had not yet answered requests for further details.

Al Jazeera reports that this may be the first time a US soldier has been suspected of spying for a foreign government while stationed in the UK. The case follows other arrests. In October, British police detained three men on suspicion of aiding Russian intelligence, and a month before that three people were held on suspicion of spying for Moscow. In September, a British man appeared in a London court accused of plotting to sabotage drone factories for Russian military intelligence.

Britain has been among the most vocal supporters of Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and its ties with Moscow are at a low ebb. Russian-linked espionage on British soil predates the war, including the 2006 poisoning of former spy Alexander Litvinenko in London and a 2018 plot to kill double agent Sergei Skripal with poison in Salisbury.
items.cav: No charges have been announced, and none of the allegations has been tested in court. The sources differ on how the barracks is described, and the FBI arrest figures come only from Patel’s own statement. Where the suspect is held and the details of his posting are second-hand reporting.
items.op: Allegations of espionage against a serving soldier must be tested in open court, not in press briefings. Public confidence depends on clarity about the legal basis for holding him and the evidence behind the accusations. Governments that ask for trust on national security should first show their working.

items.t: House Republicans block effort to impeach Pete Hegseth over US military operations
items.s: Republicans in the House of Representatives have blocked an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which cited US military actions in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela. Hegseth has dismissed the move as political theatre.
p: House Republicans have blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, according to the Guardian’s First Thing briefing. The measure was put forward by a Republican lawmaker, Thomas Massie, and the Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution before the vote.

Massie’s 34-page resolution, which he read aloud on the House floor, centred on the war with Iran. It also cited strikes in Yemen, attacks on alleged drug boats and the capture of Venezuela’s former leader, Nicolás Maduro, the briefing said.

Hegseth rejected the resolution. He called it “political spectacle” and said it was an attempt to set up a “show trial”. He also argued that the articles targeted not only him but also the troops who carried out his orders.

Hegseth insisted that every operation cited was lawful, had been ordered by President Donald Trump and had been notified to Congress. Those are his own assertions, and the briefing does not describe any independent review of them. The resolution’s specific allegations, as summarised, are the lawmaker’s claims, not findings.

The episode comes as Republicans are regrouping after sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections, according to the same briefing. The Guardian’s summary does not say how many Republicans voted for the referral or whether the judiciary committee will take up the matter.

Whatever the political calculations, the central question is simple: when a cabinet secretary faces serious allegations about how the country goes to war, Congress has a duty to examine them openly. Referring a resolution to committee can be a legitimate step, but it must lead to real scrutiny, with records made available and the public told what was found.
items.cav: This account rests on a single newsletter summary, not on the full text of the resolution, the vote or the committee’s response. Hegseth’s claims that the operations were lawful are his own and are not independently verified in the source.
items.op: Serious questions about war powers should not be settled by procedure alone. Congress owes the public a transparent examination of every operation cited, and a referral that ends without records or findings would be a failure of accountability.

items.t: House Republicans block Hegseth impeachment push, but Democrats vow to revive it in January
items.s: A bid to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has been effectively shelved for now after the House voted to send it to a Republican-led committee. Democrats say the matter is not over and plan to take it up when they control Congress.
p: The House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 to refer impeachment articles against Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, a move that effectively halts the effort for the rest of this Congress. According to the BBC, every Republican except Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie voted with the majority. Massie, a critic of the president within his own party, introduced the eight articles on Monday.

The articles accuse Hegseth of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, which Massie said had lasted more than 90 days. They also allege “extrajudicial killings” in US strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean, and refer to the 2025 conflict with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Euronews reports that Massie also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech after he tried to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging service members to resist illegal orders.

Speaking at a Pentagon briefing, his first in six months according to the BBC, Hegseth called the effort a “farce” and a “stunt” and described it as sabotage. He argued that Massie was motivated by policy disagreements rather than the offences the framers of the Constitution had in mind. He also said the resolution signalled to US adversaries that the country would punish its own personnel for lawful operations.

President Donald Trump praised the result on Truth Social, saying the effort had “miserably FAILED” and calling Hegseth a “Great American Patriot”. Vice President JD Vance said Hegseth had “obviously not” committed impeachable offences. Massie said he was disappointed but not surprised, and said members of Congress knew what to do but would not act, even when it would help them politically.

Several Democrats missed the vote, and more than a dozen members were absent in total, including 11 Democrats, some of whom blamed traffic. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed criticised them publicly, saying, “You should show up and do your job.”

The outcome is not final. Democrats are set to take control of both chambers in January after their midterm gains, and impeachment resolutions can carry over past the end of a congressional term. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said, “This is not the end of it.” Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, will leave Congress and will not be part of that next phase.

Euronews frames the vote against a wider backdrop of public discontent over the Iran war, high gas prices and the cost of living, which it links to the party’s midterm defeat. The BBC does not draw that connection, and neither report provides polling to show how widely those concerns are shared.
items.cav: Both outlets rely on Massie’s own description of the articles and on Hegseth’s rebuttal; the allegations have not been tested in committee or court. Euronews suggests a formal charge vote had been expected on Wednesday, a detail the BBC does not mention, so it is unclear whether that timetable was ever firm.
items.op: Whatever one thinks of Hegseth, accusations that a war ran for months without congressional approval deserve a full hearing, not a procedural burial. Sending the articles to a committee chaired by allies of the president shields the question from scrutiny. Congress owes the public a recorded answer, and deferring it to January only postpones that obligation.

items.t: Germany reportedly bans Chinese-made drones from military bases over security fears
items.s: Germany has reportedly barred off-the-shelf Chinese drones from its military installations, citing security risks. The step adds to a broader Western unease about Chinese technology in sensitive settings.
p: According to reports, Berlin has prohibited commercially sold drones made in China from its army bases and training areas. The restriction is said to apply with immediate effect.

Der Spiegel reported that military units bought these drones in recent years with little formal scrutiny. The magazine said they are now being pulled from use as fast as possible. At the time of reporting, the defence ministry had not responded to a request for comment.

Under a 2024 procurement strategy, local commanders were permitted to purchase drones from a list of approved models, and several of the listed systems came from DJI, a China-based manufacturer that the report describes as the largest of its kind. Because no central register tracks what individual units have bought, the military reportedly concluded that only a general prohibition would work.

Germany's move follows comparable decisions elsewhere. In February, Poland stopped Chinese-built vehicles from entering its military sites over fears that onboard sensors could harvest sensitive information, although such vehicles may still be admitted once certain functions are switched off. The US military has likewise barred BYD electric cars from Kadena airbase on Okinawa. A US air force spokesperson described the danger as an “unmitigable risk”, but American officials have not pointed to a specific threat.

Concern has also reached everyday consumer technology. In September, the Dutch government cautioned that built-in features such as microphones, cameras and location trackers in modern cars could let hostile governments spy on drivers. The advisory did not name any country or carmaker. Last week, a group of European lawmakers asked the European Commission to examine whether BYD vehicles pose a threat and whether they should be excluded from public contracts. Fourteen parliamentarians also asked the EU cybersecurity agency to weigh listing BYD as a high-risk supplier, and French MEP François Kalfon argued that China's 2017 intelligence law obliges firms to assist the state.

BYD responded that data handled by its vehicles, whether stored in the cloud or on board, cannot be accessed remotely from China, and that owners keep control over their information. The company said BYD Europe does not provide such data to affiliates or outside parties in China.
The restrictions are not without precedent. In 2018 the US defence department banned Huawei and ZTE smartphones from military bases worldwide, also on security grounds.
