items.cav: The German ban comes second-hand via Der Spiegel, and Berlin's defence ministry had not commented. The sources name no specific threat, and BYD rejects the data concerns raised about its vehicles.
items.op: Protecting military sites from foreign surveillance is legitimate, but blanket bans born of missing records point to a governance failure rather than a strategy. Germany should publish the criteria behind its drone decision and the specific risks it addresses. Without that transparency, security measures risk looking like improvisation.

items.t: Ukraine and Russia continue US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi as territory remains the main obstacle
items.s: Negotiators from Ukraine and Russia are back at the table in Abu Dhabi under US mediation. Kyiv says it sees a shift in Washington’s stance, but disputes over land and the terms of a ceasefire persist.
p: Talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, were set to continue in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday for a second day. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking to journalists in Copenhagen on Tuesday, said he had noticed a change in how American mediators were handling the process and that he was pleased with what he had heard. So far, however, neither side has announced a deal.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the negotiations as productive. Envoy Jared Kushner claimed Washington had reduced the distance between the two delegations, though he gave no specifics. Such upbeat remarks have not concealed the gulf between Kyiv and Moscow over land and the conditions for halting the fighting.

Discussions on Wednesday were expected to cover de-escalation steps, including energy infrastructure and the Black Sea, as well as the possibility of a three-way meeting at leader level. Territory is the thorniest issue. Moscow wants Ukrainian forces to pull out of eastern areas, including places Kyiv still holds.

According to Zelenskyy, Russian negotiators wrongly asserted that their forces had seized half of the Donbas territory Ukraine still controls. Ukraine’s team answered with video footage. General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, who was also in Abu Dhabi, reportedly confirmed that Ukrainian battlefield maps were more accurate, Zelenskyy said. The president also argued that Vladimir Putin may be receiving misleading information about Russian advances, and insisted that land questions must ultimately be decided by leaders rather than negotiators.

Before the talks, Donald Trump indicated that Ukraine may have to accept some territorial adjustments, saying the country would end up with “a little bit different shape”. Washington and Moscow also want to address wider European security arrangements. Kushner spoke of a new framework covering Ukraine, Russia and Europe, while a source in the Russian delegation said ending the war was only one of Moscow’s objectives.

European officials have held separate consultations in Abu Dhabi but are excluded from the three-party format. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov dismissed their presence, saying they could “sit there in the hotel”. Rubio countered that Europe would eventually have to take part, as it forms part of the solution. Moscow still refuses an immediate ceasefire, and Lavrov accused European governments of giving Kyiv time to rebuild its forces.

So far, the only concrete outcomes have come from humanitarian work and prisoner exchanges. Kyiv hopes limited truces could open the way to a wider ceasefire, pointing to last month’s operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, which enabled aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. Zelenskyy said both sides are weighing an exchange of 1,000 prisoners each, or possibly 1,500, with US officials expected to travel to Russia. A similar 1,000-for-1,000 arrangement was agreed in Istanbul in May 2025, but no new deal has been formally announced.
items.cav: This report rests on a single outlet and relies heavily on Zelenskyy’s own account, including his claims about Russian statements and the battlefield maps Grynkewich reportedly confirmed. Kushner and Rubio offered no specifics, and the prisoner figures are described as under discussion rather than agreed.
items.op: Peace talks that touch borders and security cannot succeed on vague praise alone. Kyiv, Moscow, Washington and European capitals should publish the terms they are actually weighing so the public can judge them. Territorial changes agreed only by leaders, without open scrutiny, would deserve little trust.

items.t: UK foreign secretary says climate crisis now threatens national security ahead of Cop31
items.s: Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, plans to tell leaders at the Cop31 summit in Turkey that climate breakdown is now a direct threat to security everywhere. He made the case in an interview with the Guardian before his Wednesday speech.
p: Miliband contends that defence and security concerns should now sit at the centre of climate policy. In his account, rapid warming is driving food shortages, economic upheaval, displacement and conflict. Scenarios that once belonged to science fiction, he says, now appear in routine news coverage.

He told the paper that food supply, infrastructure and population movements are already being affected by the crisis. He also took aim at the Conservatives and Reform UK, both of which the article says want to abandon efforts to cut emissions. Those who avoid the issue, he argued, are endangering national security.

The Cop31 talks in Antalya opened on Monday and run for two weeks. The leaders’ segment takes place on Wednesday and Thursday, and Miliband landed in Turkey on Tuesday evening. Australia’s Anthony Albanese and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan will open that segment, with addresses also planned from António Guterres, Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed, whose country hosts next year’s meeting.

Several major leaders are staying away, among them China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz. Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, will attend. Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, is due to travel on Wednesday and hold talks with counterparts on Thursday.

Miliband is expected to say that overshooting the 1.5C limit above preindustrial temperatures is now effectively unavoidable. The planet has been above that level for two years and is unlikely to cool much. That, he will argue, calls for tougher policies to stop warming speeding up, and for ways to bring temperatures back to safer levels over the coming decades.

He links fossil fuel price shocks to the surge in oil prices this year after the Iran war began, a rise that has fed inflation and interest rate increases by central banks. He describes such shocks as routine now, and wants governments to redouble efforts to cut emissions and build resilience, alongside more clean energy investment, action on methane and forest protection.

According to the article, campaigners say Burnham’s government is drifting from the UK’s net zero target for 2050. They point to plans to loosen a requirement on carmakers to sell more electric vehicles by 2030, approval for the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, and possible licensing of the Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland. The article does not include a government response.
items.cav: Miliband’s comments come from an interview given before his speech, so they are his stated positions rather than delivered remarks. The criticism of government policy is the claim of campaigners, and the article gives no government reply. The claim that the 1.5C overshoot is inevitable is presented as Miliband’s assessment.
items.op: Framing climate policy as a security question forces governments to weigh costs they already pay. But a minister who warns of catastrophe while his government clears a new gasfield and weakens electric vehicle rules owes the public a clear account of how those choices fit together. Transparency on that trade-off is the real test.

items.t: Ukraine, Russia and US resume Abu Dhabi peace talks as Black Sea attacks continue
items.s: Ukraine, Russia and the United States have begun a second day of talks in Abu Dhabi, following a first round that Kyiv called encouraging. According to Euronews, a prisoner exchange and security guarantees are under discussion.
p: Euronews reports that the negotiations are advancing after an opening day that Kyiv viewed favourably. Its correspondent Sasha Vakulina looks at what each side has publicly said and whether their stances are converging.

NATO is represented in the Emirati capital by General Alexus Grynkewich. Speaking to Euronews, John Stringer, the alliance's Deputy Supreme Allied Commander, was asked whether he sees real room for a breakthrough.

Separately, Euronews defence correspondent Angela Skujins explained that Brussels intends to direct €70 million toward the Black Sea area, where vessels are reportedly being hit and sailors remain unaccounted for. The report did not identify who is behind the strikes.

The same programme also covered Europe’s hybrid threats. Riho Terras, a European People’s Party member of the European Parliament from Estonia, questioned whether the continent is doing enough to protect itself. Euronews also reported on Prince Harry’s speech in Strasbourg, Meghan’s visit, and a “Lost Screen Memorial” honouring young people whose deaths have been linked to online harms.
items.cav: The source is a daily briefing preview, not a report of outcomes. It does not say what was agreed, what the prisoner exchange involves, or who is responsible for the Black Sea attacks. The description of the talks as positive comes from Kyiv.
items.op: Peace talks deserve scrutiny only if their terms can be checked. Any security guarantees or prisoner exchange reached in Abu Dhabi should be published in full, so civilians and seafarers can judge whether the process protects them or merely pauses the fighting.

items.t: Mona Chalabi’s ‘Ten Lives’ asks what happens when Americans open their finances to view
items.s: In a first book that mixes journalism, data visualisation and memoir, former Guardian data journalist Mona Chalabi argues that secrecy about personal income sustains an unfair system. The book follows ten Americans across the income spectrum, plus the author herself.
p: Mona Chalabi, a former Guardian data journalist and illustrator, has written a first book that puts personal finances under scrutiny. According to the review in The Guardian, Ten Lives follows ten individual Americans over a five-year period and explores how their wealth, or lack of it, has shaped their lives.

The subjects were chosen to represent the full range of the US income ladder. Chalabi asks readers to imagine every American lined up from poorest to richest and divided into ten equal groups. Each interviewee comes from one of those groups, so all ten steps are depicted. The reviewer describes a New York investment banker who keeps his money in an elastic band, a former teen gambling addict trying to rebuild his life, and a newly divorced graduate student who considers surrogacy to afford childcare.

Chalabi also includes herself as an eleventh subject. The review says she discloses the size of her advance for the book, provides a spreadsheet of her freelance earnings, and admits she was able to buy a five-bedroom home in London for more than £1.5m. She acknowledges discomfort as a social justice advocate who has become rich.

The reviewer praises the book’s frankness and its direct prose, including Chalabi’s criticism of George Orwell’s writing on poverty. Her central argument, as quoted in the review, is that collective ignorance about individual income sustains an unfair system, and that people who refuse to discuss their money cannot tackle the insecurity many feel.

According to the review, the stories show how problems such as the lack of affordable healthcare and childcare can upend lives. Chalabi says her own savings went to care for her mother after a stroke in the UK. She links the fear shared by all eleven subjects to what she calls the corrosive individualism of advanced capitalism.

Chalabi concludes that financial security depends on a well-funded safety net covering healthcare, education and welfare. Rather than focusing only on billionaires, she suggests, people should start by being more open about their own wealth and their reliance on one another. The reviewer calls the argument brilliant and radical.
items.cav: This is a single review, so the book’s contents are described second-hand and the reviewer’s assessment is not independently verified. The review does not give details of the subjects’ current circumstances beyond the five-year period.
items.op: Chalabi is right that silence about money protects those who benefit from opacity. If public institutions are to be funded fairly, citizens need to know who earns what and who pays. Transparency should not stop at the billionaires’ door, and it should start with those who campaign against inequality.
